title: Tailscale SSH security update and mitigation steps
excerpt: Tailscale is fixing privilege-escalation bugs in SSH and advises temporary config changes until the patched client ships.
body:
Tailscale’s SSH feature recently ran into a set of privilege-escalation bugs. The issue shows up when a device that is already allowed to connect over Tailscale SSH also has SSH forwarding turned on. In a handful of host configurations that combination lets the device run commands or forward traffic beyond the rights of the local user it is mapped to.

The engineering and security teams dug into the problem with help from external specialists. Their investigation uncovered three conditions that make exploitation possible: the permissions granted to the connecting user or device, whether SSH forwarding is enabled, and the host’s overall configuration.

The source does not say every Tailscale SSH deployment is vulnerable, and it does not advise a blanket shutdown of the feature. Instead, the team is accelerating remediation work and publishing short-term guidance for customers who need protection today.

This post will show what the investigation found, what fixes are on the way, which mitigations can be applied right now, and what to watch for until the patched client lands.

## Most of the issues involve privilege escalation  

In the scenarios the team observed, an authorized client can forward a connection or invoke a command that bypasses the local user’s permissions. The result is that the client can act with higher privileges on the target host. Exploitation depends on the specific access policies in place and on whether SSH forwarding is permitted. The engineers are still mapping the full scope of affected configurations, but the current assessment shows that the vulnerability is not universal.

## Fixes are being tested and a release is planned  

Engineers have already implemented fixes for the majority of the findings. Testing is underway, and a patched client is slated for release by the end of Tuesday 27 October, assuming the tests pass.

When the client lands, Tailscale will publish a security advisory that lists the confirmed vulnerabilities, the affected versions, and the steps needed to remediate them. A follow-up technical blog post will explain the root causes and the engineering changes that were made. The source for this timeline is the Tailscale SSH: Investigation and remediation update page[^1].

## Short-term configuration mitigations  

While the patch is in flight, Tailscale recommends a short list of actions that can be applied today to reduce risk.

1. Review SSH access policies, limit access to the users and devices that truly need it. Tightening policies shrinks the attack surface.  
2. Disable SSH forwarding if it isn’t required, set the environment variable `TS_SSH_DISABLE_FORWARDING=1` in the `tailscaled` service and restart the service. This turns off forwarding without disabling Tailscale SSH entirely and mitigates several of the more serious findings.

   ```bash
   export TS_SSH_DISABLE_FORWARDING=1
   systemctl restart tailscaled
   ```

3. Restrict access to sensitive systems, temporarily tighten policies for high-value machines so that only a narrow set of users and devices can reach them via SSH.  
4. Prepare to update, monitor the release announcement and plan to roll out the patched client as soon as it becomes available.

These steps address the most exploitable paths without requiring a full feature shutdown.

## What customers should watch for  

The upcoming advisory will detail the exact versions that are vulnerable, the configurations that are at risk, and the remediation steps once the patched client is released. Until then, customers should keep an eye on the Tailscale status page and the support channel for any changes to the timeline or additional guidance. Environments with permissive SSH policies or heavy reliance on forwarding should prioritize the mitigations above.

## The takeaway  

The current Tailscale SSH vulnerability hinges on SSH forwarding and permissive access policies. Until the patched client ships, disable forwarding with `TS_SSH_DISABLE_FORWARDING=1` and tighten SSH policies. Applying those steps now blocks the most dangerous paths while the official fix is finalized.

[^1]: https://tailscale.com/ssh-investigation-update
